chunks: Follow your Prophet, the purest, the most chaste (peace be upon him and his family).
For in him is an example for the follower, and a consolation for the seeker of consolation.
The most beloved of servants to Allah is he who follows His Prophet, and who treads in his footsteps.
He took the least (share) from this world and did not take a full glance at it.
Of all the people of the world he was the least satiated and the most empty of stomach.
The world was offered to him but he refused to accept it.
When he knew that Allah, the Glorified, hated a thing, he too hated it; that Allah held a thing low, he too held it low; that Allah held a thing small, he too held it small.
If we love what Allah and His Prophet hate and hold great what Allah and His prophet hold small that would be enough isolation from Allah and transgression of His commands.

key_terms.أَهْضَمُ: The least satiated or most humble
key_terms.الْمُقْتَصُّ: One who follows closely in the footsteps
key_terms.قَضَمَ الدُّنْيَا: To take a small share of the world

ai.seo_question: How does following the Prophet's example lead to being beloved to Allah?
ai.summary: In this passage from Nahj al-Balagha, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) presents the Prophet Muhammad as the epitome of *zuhd* (asceticism), describing his rejection of the world not as mere indifference but as an active, profound disengagement that earned him the title of the most humble among people. This aligns with the Shia scholarly emphasis on *ittiba'* (following) the Prophet's character as the primary means of attaining divine proximity, where love for the Prophet becomes a direct reflection of love for God. The text underscores that the Prophet’s alignment with Divine will—loving what God loves and hating what He hates—serves as the ultimate model for believers to emulate in their spiritual journey.
